content: The common cold is an infection of the upper respiratory tract that resolves on its own. It is characterized by symptoms such as a runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, coughing, malaise, sore throat, and occasionally fever, which is typically below 37.8°C. While the common cold is generally not considered harmful, it imposes a significant economic burden due to missed school and workdays. In the United States, the economic impact of the common cold is estimated to exceed $40 billion annually. This includes approximately 70 million workdays missed by employees, 189 million school days missed by children, and 126 million workdays missed by parents caring for sick children. In Europe, the cost per episode of the common cold can reach up to €1102. Additionally, there is substantial spending on inappropriate antimicrobial prescriptions for this condition. Developing vaccines for the common cold has proven challenging due to the antigenic variability of the viruses responsible for the illness. In some cases, bacteria can also act as causative agents. There remains uncertainty regarding the efficacy and safety of interventions aimed at preventing the common cold in healthy individuals. This review was conducted to update previous Cochrane Reviews published in 2011, 2013, and 2017, with the objective of assessing the clinical effectiveness and safety of vaccines for preventing the common cold in healthy people. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and LILACS, covering literature up to April 2022. Additional searches were performed in trial registries and other websites. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared any virus vaccine with a placebo for the prevention of the common cold in healthy individuals. The initial search results were screened using Cochrane’s Screen4Me workflow. Four review authors independently reviewed titles and abstracts to identify potentially relevant studies. Full-text articles of potentially relevant studies were retrieved and independently assessed for inclusion. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third review author. Data extraction was performed independently by two review authors, and any disagreements were resolved by consensus or with the involvement of a third author. Data were double-checked and analyzed using Review Manager 5 software. Risk of bias was assessed using the RoB 1 tool, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADEpro GDT software. A summary of findings table was created. However, no meta-analysis was conducted, and publication bias was not assessed. This updated review did not identify any new RCTs for inclusion. The review includes a single RCT conducted in 1965, which had a high risk of bias. The study involved 2307 healthy young men in a military facility and compared the effects of three adenovirus vaccines (live, inactivated type 4, and inactivated type 4 and 7) with a placebo (either a physiological saline injection or a gelatin capsule). In the vaccine group, 13 events (1.14%) were reported among 1139 participants, while 14 events (1.19%) occurred among 1168 participants in the placebo group. The results do not provide clear evidence of a difference between the adenovirus vaccine and placebo in reducing the incidence of the common cold (risk ratio 0.95, 95% confidence interval 0.45 to 2.02; very low-certainty evidence). Additionally, no differences in adverse events were reported when comparing the live vaccine preparation with the placebo. The certainty of the evidence was downgraded to very low due to unclear risk of bias, indirectness (as the study population consisted solely of young men), and imprecision (due to wide confidence intervals and a low number of events). The study did not assess vaccine-related or all-cause mortality. In conclusion, this Cochrane Review is based on a single study with very low-certainty evidence, which suggests that there may be no difference between the adenovirus vaccine and placebo in reducing the incidence of the common cold. There is a clear need for well-designed, adequately powered RCTs to investigate vaccines for the common cold in healthy individuals. Future trials should evaluate a variety of virus vaccines and measure outcomes such as the incidence of the common cold, vaccine safety, and both all-cause and vaccine-related mortality.
